[Admin note: The specific card effects have changed across the four editions of Innovation, in addition to age 11 being added in the fourth edition, but the core gameplay has remained consistent across all editions, so all editions are listed on a single page in the database.]

ai.summary: Innovation is a fast-paced tableau-builder where you race through ages of technology, splaying cards to reveal icons and chaining dogpile combos that can swing the game in a single turn. It's brutally interactive despite having no board or dice — you're constantly reading opponents' tableaus and timing when to demand, share, or rush an achievement before they do.
praised: Incredible depth and replayability from a small deck of cards
Elegant, tightly integrated rules where every card's effect ties into its theme
Explosive, satisfying combo turns once you see the engine click
Fast to play and easy to reset for another game
criticised: Steep learning curve and dense rules text on cards makes early games confusing
Can feel swingy or 'solved' by a single big combo that ends the game abruptly
Kingmaking and analysis paralysis in multiplayer as players parse others' boards
Iconography and card interactions are hard to teach to new players

interaction.kind: sharing/demanding effects and tableau disruption (take that)

scoring.why: The game is won by claiming achievements (via score thresholds or special criteria), not by tallying broad point sources, so a single well-timed combo or dogma chain usually decides the winner.

name: Innovation Ultimate
description:
Innovation Ultimate is a box set containing Innovation and all five of its expansions, which includes a brand new expansion titled The Unseen.

Many, many updates have been made to this edition. First, Age 11 has been added, representing the recent past and potential near future at the time of release. Language and mechanics have been streamlined, and in particular, the expansions have all been heavily reworked to be more accessible and easy to include while playing.
families: Versions & Editions: Big Box Versions of Individual Games

ai.summary: Innovation is a fast, brain-burning card game where you build tech trees and constantly steal or copy each other's effects via chained 'dogma' actions, so a quiet turn can suddenly cascade into your opponent's cards firing repeatedly against you. This Ultimate edition bundles the base game with all five expansions plus a new Age 11 and reworked rules, making an already dense engine even bigger and more combo-laden.
praised: Explosive, satisfying combos and chain reactions once you see the engine click
Extremely fast to play despite deep strategic depth
High replayability from asymmetric card effects and splaying
Clever theme expressed through card icons and history-themed names
This edition's rules streamlining and consolidation of all expansions in one box
criticised: Steep learning curve; card text is famously hard to parse for new players
Can feel like solitaire with occasional interference rather than direct interaction
Snowballing/kingmaking issues, especially at higher player counts
Analysis paralysis from tracking everyone's board and available dogma actions
Adding all expansions plus Age 11 raises complexity/rules overhead further

interaction.kind: sharing and stealing dogma effects, take-that card/resource disruption

scoring.why: Winning comes from reaching achievement thresholds or accumulating enough score-value icons through a tuned tech-tree engine, not from summing unrelated scoring categories

name: Inventions: Evolution of Ideas
description:
Since the dawn of time, humanity has sought new ideas, forever developing them into still newer concepts. Their genius made them stand out from the other animals. Each invention is a veritable evolutionary step. Humans' use of tools surpasses the efforts of all others, making Homo sapiens technologists since before historical records were invented.

Inventions: Evolution of Ideas follows humanity's most noteworthy innovations and places the power of these technological developments in your hands to evolve your societies over the ages.

In Inventions, cards simulate these new concepts. Cards are the ideas that eventually become inventions. Once they are invented, these technologies can be shared with the world, and everyone involved in the process spreads the exciting news, giving credit where credit is due. Developing these inventions progresses your society, advancing its technology, economy, and culture. You can even share with other societies, boosting the inventions' efficacy even more!

Inventions is a tactical game, but you will do best by building these tactics around a long-term strategy. Each society's progress will be measured in Intellectual Property Points (IPP), and the player who has the most IPP has the strongest society and wins the game.

ai.summary: A dense Vital Lacerda worker-placement engine-builder where you develop invention cards through stages (idea to invention to global spread), pulling levers across several interlocking boards to generate Intellectual Property Points. Turns are quiet and heads-down as each player optimizes their own engine, with occasional friction over shared worker-placement spots and card availability.
praised: Tight, elegant interlocking systems typical of Lacerda's design
Strong sense of building an engine and watching it snowball
High replayability from variable inventions and multiple viable paths to points
Satisfying puzzle of sequencing actions efficiently
Solo mode is well regarded
criticised: Steep rules overhead and long teach/setup time
Heavy iconography that takes several plays to internalize
Analysis paralysis due to the number of simultaneous considerations
Low direct interaction can make multiplayer feel like parallel solitaire
High cost of entry (price, table space) for a niche heavy-gamer audience

interaction.kind: mostly parallel engine-building with light blocking over shared worker spots and card draft

scoring.why: IPP accumulates from multiple systems (developing and spreading inventions, technology/economy/culture tracks, and bonus objectives), so the winner is whoever best diversifies and chains these scoring avenues

name: Irish Gauge
description:
Irish Gauge — one of three titles in Winsome Games 2014 Essen Set — is played on a map of Ireland and is similar in style to many of the stock-based, cube-rail games released by Winsome Games since 2007.

On each player's turn, they can either place a share of one of five companies up for auction, build track (represented by cubes) in one of these five companies, upgrade a town to a city, or call for dividends. The dividends are paid out to shareholders of certain railroads based on how many cities/towns they connect to and how many shares of this company have been issued. The upgrade and dividend actions also affect game length and the likelihood of further dividends for each company. The game ends when a certain condition is met at the end of a player's turn, and the player with the highest sum of money and stock value at the end of this turn wins.

Irish Gauge is the first title in the Iron Rail series by Capstone Games.
families: Misc: Watch It Played How To Videos

ai.summary: A tight, fast-playing cube-rail auction game where players bid on shares, build track, and time dividend calls to maximize their own stock value while starving rivals of income; games run under an hour but every auction and build decision is loaded with opportunity cost. It's considered one of the best entry points into the Winsome/18xx-style stock-and-rail genre because of its short length and clean rules.
praised: Short playtime relative to the depth of decisions
Tense, meaningful share auctions where price-setting matters as much as buying
Good gateway into 18xx-style stock/rail mechanics without the complexity
High replayability from variable company performance each game
criticised: Can feel swingy or luck-influenced by which companies randomly draw good routes
Runaway leader potential if one player dominates early share/track decisions
Thin theme, essentially an abstract economic puzzle
Some feel it's overshadowed by other titles in the same Winsome/Iron Rail lineage

interaction.kind: auction bidding and share/track competition

scoring.why: The winner is whoever ends with the highest combined cash and stock value, driven mainly by smart auction timing and dividend calls

name: Ishtar: Gardens of Babylon
description:
From the award-winning designer Bruno Cathala, Ishtar is a game in which you play the role of a gardener aiming to transform the dry desert into the Lost Hanging Gardens of Babylon. To accomplish your mission, you will have to plant flowers, which, if you place them well, can help you gather precious gems and activate actions. Whether to buy Trees (which will block the link between two Flower spots, as well as earning you points) or to purchase upgrades (such as getting two more points per Tree card at the end of the game), collecting gems will be a crucial part of the game. Get them before your opponents, recruit apprentices, send them to earn points in the copses of flowers you have created, block others and think carefully of the upgrades to purchase if you want to become the best gardener at the end of the game!

—description from the publisher

ai.summary: Ishtar is a tight, puzzly rondel-and-tile-placement game where you plant flowers to trigger chained bonuses, then race to claim gem-based scoring conditions before opponents beat you to them. Turns are quick but the board state is tense, since good flower placements are contested and trees can cut off your opponents' combos.
praised: Clever, tight rondel mechanism that constrains choices meaningfully
Satisfying chain-reaction flower placement puzzle
Fast turns keep the game moving despite the thinking involved
Attractive, colorful production
Good player count scalability, plays well at 2
criticised: Can feel a bit dry or abstract despite the gardening theme
Some player interaction is more about racing/blocking than direct engagement, which can feel solitaire-ish at times
Upgrade/gem economy can be hard to parse for new players
Limited replayability variance once strategies are known

interaction.kind: blocking and area denial via tree placement and racing for gem thresholds

scoring.why: Points come from trees, apprentice scoring in flower copses, and upgrade bonuses, but efficient combo-chaining on the rondel decides the winner

name: Istanbul: Big Box
description:
Istanbul: Big Box is the all-in-one package for Istanbul, including the base game as well as both expansions, Mocha & Baksheesh and Letters & Seals. It also includes the Istanbul: Caravan Leader Mini Expansion, in the form of a small tile rather than a camel meeple.

This combination also gives players the option to play on a big 5 x 5 tiles bazaar.
families: Versions & Editions: Big Box Versions of Individual Games

ai.summary: Istanbul is a tight pick-up-and-deliver game where you move your merchant and assistants around a modular grid of place tiles, leaving assistants behind to trigger repeatable actions while racing to collect rubies for scoring. It plays fast and tense despite the calm theme, with efficient route-planning and light blocking as other players occupy the tiles you need.
praised: Tight, tense action-efficiency puzzle despite simple rules
Modular board gives high replayability and varied setups
Quick turns keep downtime low even at higher player counts
Big Box bundles both expansions plus mini-expansion at good value and improves component quality/insert
criticised: Can feel a bit dry or 'mechanical' thematically
Assistant-placement blocking can occasionally lead to slight kingmaking or bad luck if a needed tile is occupied
Some find the base game a bit light at higher weight expectations; the 5x5 big bazaar mode with more players can drag
Expansions (esp. Letters & Seals) add complexity that not all groups want

interaction.kind: tile/space blocking and light area denial via assistant placement

ai.win_criteria: Most points, one or two sources

scoring.why: The winner is decided almost entirely by rubies collected, with bonus tiles/wheelbarrow upgrades acting as accelerants rather than separate scoring tracks

name: It's a Wonderful World
description:
In It’s a Wonderful World, you are an expanding Empire and must choose your path to your future. You must develop faster and better than your competitors. You’ll carefully plan your expansion to develop your production power and rule over this new world.

It’s a Wonderful World is a cards drafting and engine building game from 1 to 5 players. Each round, players will draft 7 cards and then choose which ones will be recycled to immediately acquire Resources, and which ones will be kept for construction to produce Resources each round and/or gain victory points.

When a card is fully built, it’s added to the player’s Empire to increase the player’s production capacity for each round. The mechanical twist being that the production phase works in a specific order. You'll have to plan your constructions carefully!

For a deeper insight of the gameplay, please follow this link : It's a Wonderful World - First steps

In addition to the base game, players can also enjoy expansions boxes introducing an innovative Campaign mode. Each Campaign offers a storyline to follow and many gameplay twists. At the end of each campaign, players will open a reward booster to unlock new cards, enhance their base game and keep a memory of what happened during the campaign. All the campaigns can be replayed and don’t imply game components destruction.

More info on the Campaign mode : It's a Wonderful World - Campaign Mode 

—description from the publisher

ai.summary: It's a Wonderful World is a card-drafting engine-builder where you draft from a hand, then simultaneously decide which cards to recycle for resources versus construct for ongoing production and points. The tense part is that production resolves in a fixed resource order each round, so timing your engine and covering shortfalls (or converting excess via recycling) is the core puzzle.
praised: Efficient simultaneous-play drafting means little downtime despite being a drafting game
Satisfying engine-building puzzle with meaningful tension between recycling now vs building for later
Strong solo mode
Attractive production and thematic sci-fi/civilization art
Scales well and plays quickly for the amount of decision-making involved
criticised: Can feel like a multiplayer solitaire with limited direct interaction beyond drafting
Some randomness in what cards appear can swing a game
Rules around production order and resource conversion have a learning curve for new players
Later plays can feel a bit samey without expansions

interaction.kind: drafting against opponents but mostly parallel engine-building

scoring.why: Points come from multiple card types (empire cards, achievements, bonuses) so the winner is whoever builds the most efficient, well-timed production engine

name: Just One
description:
Just One is a co-operative party game in which you all play together to get the best score! Your goal each round is to get one player — the active player — to guess a mystery word based on the clues given by teammates. Can you achieve a perfect score by guessing all the mystery words?

In more detail, everyone who is not the active player sees the mystery word, then each player independently writes a clue on their personal easel. Once everyone has finished, you reveal the clues to one another. All identical clues are removed from play, so try to be original!

After eliminating duplicate clues, reveal the remaining clues to the active player. If they correctly guess the mystery word, your team scores a point. If they decline to guess, you don't score the current card. If they guess wrong, you don't score the current card and you lose one of the points you had already scored. Thus, be original, but not so original that you don't help the active player guess correctly!
families: Components: Dry Erase Markers / Dry Erase Surfaces
Mechanism: Give a Clue / Get a Clue

ai.summary: Just One is a fast, low-stress cooperative party game where the table quietly compares one-word clues and giggles over near-misses and duplicate wipeouts; there's no real strategy, just word association and trying to read your teammates' minds. It plays best as a light, inclusive icebreaker that works across a wide range of ages and group sizes.
praised: Extremely easy to teach and get running in under a minute
Generates a lot of laughter, especially from unintentionally duplicate or wildly off-base clues
Fully cooperative so there's no downtime tension or player elimination
Scales well from small to large groups and works with mixed skill/age levels
Great value/production for a small box
criticised: Little to no strategic depth, so it can feel thin for gamers looking for a 'real' game
Luck of word association means a good guesser can still fail on a bad card
Replayability can dip once the included word cards are exhausted
Some groups find it too light or repetitive after several sessions

interaction.kind: Simultaneous clue-writing and shared deduction toward one guesser

scoring.why: The team's single running score is simply the count of mystery words correctly guessed minus the ones guessed wrong, so there's no 'winner' beyond the group's shared tally.

name: Kanban EV
description:
Electric vehicles (EVs) have become more common since 2014 and are the future of the automobile industry. They are superior vehicles due to them being more efficient, easier to maintain, cleaner, and cheaper to run. They are computerized machines that use AI to improve safety and in the near future will provide autonomous driving. They receive software upgrades during their lifetime and are constantly improving, unlike their traditional combustion-engine counterparts, which start to become obsolete as soon as you start using them.

You will be overseeing the production of these vehicles in Kanban EV, with "kanban" (看板) being the name for a scheduling system that supports an efficient assembly line, just-in-time production, and a smooth workflow process. Over the course of the game, players take on the role of rookie employees who are trying to secure their career. You need to manage suppliers and supplies, improve and innovate automobile parts, and get your hands greasy on the assembly line in order to boost production and impress the factory manager.

You must make shrewd use of the recycling facilities and the limited factory supplies in order to appropriate parts when the suppliers come up short. Because the factory must run at optimum efficiency, production doesn't wait for you or for mistakes. Sandra, the factory manager, will review your performance and keep the factory on tempo.

Kanban EV is a game that focuses on resource and time management that puts you in the driver's seat of an entire production facility, racing for factory goals and the highest level of promotion. You earn production points (PP) for performing various actions in the game, and the player with the most PP at the end of the game wins.

—description from publisher

Includes solo mode by Dávid Turczi

ai.summary: Kanban EV is a dense, interlocking worker-placement/action-point game where you juggle multiple resource chains (car components, R&D, JIT contracts) across a tight board with heavy multi-use action spaces; turns are short but decisions are agonizing because every action interacts with several systems at once. It rewards efficient engine-building and planning several moves ahead more than direct confrontation with opponents.
praised: Tight, elegant interlocking systems where every action affects multiple resources
Strong solo mode
Streamlined and more approachable than the original Kanban: Automotive Revolution while keeping its depth
Satisfying puzzle of optimizing just-in-time production and R&D upgrades
High replayability due to multiple viable strategies
criticised: Steep learning curve and lengthy rules overhead for a new group
Can trigger significant analysis paralysis
Feels iterative rather than groundbreaking to players who already own the original Kanban
Dry, spreadsheet-like theme integration despite the EV dressing
Long teach and setup time relative to actual play tension

interaction.kind: blocking and area denial on worker placement spaces, indirect competition for shared resources/contracts

scoring.why: Points accumulate from multiple independent systems (contracts fulfilled, R&D/technology tracks, department efficiency, end-game bonuses), so the winner is usually whoever balances several engines rather than maxing one.

name: Keyflower
description:
Keyflower is a game for two to six players played over four rounds. Each round represents a season: spring, summer, autumn, and finally winter. Each player starts the game with a "home" tile and an initial team of eight workers, each of which is colored red, yellow, or blue. Workers of matching colors are used by the players to bid for tiles to add to their villages. Matching workers may alternatively be used to generate resources, skills and additional workers, not only from the player's own tiles, but also from the tiles in the other players' villages and from the new tiles being auctioned.

In spring, summer and autumn, more workers will arrive on board the Keyflower and her sister boats, with some of these workers possessing skills in the working of the key resources of iron, stone and wood. In each of these seasons, village tiles are set out at random for auction. In the winter no new workers arrive and the players select the village tiles for auction from those they received at the beginning of the game. Each winter village tile offers VPs for certain combinations of resources, skills and workers. The player whose village and workers generate the most VPs wins the game.

Keyflower presents players with many different challenges and each game will be different due to the mix of village tiles that appear in that particular game. Throughout the game, players will need to be alert to the opportunities to best utilize their various resources, transport and upgrade capability, skills and workers.

Keyflower, a joint design between Richard Breese and Sebastian Bleasdale, is the seventh game in the "Key" series from R&D Games set in the medieval "Key" land.

ai.summary: Keyflower is a clever hybrid of worker placement and auction where you bid workers to win tiles, then use those same (or other) workers to activate tiles for resources and points, including tiles in opponents' villages. The tension between using workers now versus saving them for the endgame winter bidding round is the heart of the game, and building an efficient engine across four rounds feels very satisfying.
praised: Clever double-use of workers for both bidding and activating tiles
High interaction via using resources/skills on opponents' tiles
Satisfying variable setup and modular board every game
Rewards planning and engine-building without excessive downtime
Strong tension around the winter round using only your held tiles
criticised: Can suffer from significant analysis paralysis, especially at higher player counts
Rules and icons have a learning curve for new players
Some randomness in which tiles come up for auction
Can feel like a 'take that' game to newer players unfamiliar with the shared-tile mechanic
Endgame scoring tiles can create swingy, hard-to-predict outcomes

interaction.kind: auction/bidding plus using workers on others' tiles

scoring.why: points come from a mix of resources, skills, workers, and building combinations set by winter tiles, so the winning strategy varies each game

name: Khôra: Rise of an Empire
description:
In Khôra: Rise of an Empire, each player is the head of a blossoming city-state in Ancient Greece.

On your turn, you must take 2 of the following 7 Actions: Philosophy, Legislation, Culture, Trade, Military, Politics, or Development. Choose Actions that align with your strategy, but which also work with your dice roll.

You will need to adapt your strategy constantly and strengthen your Actions by moving your markers up on your Economy, Culture, and Military Tracks.

Move up on the Taxes Track to collect highly sought-after Drachmas, the Troop Track to Explore and gather Knowledge tokens, and the Glory Track to capitalize on your Knowledge.

Unlock Achievements and, above all, make sure you have the most points at the end of the 9th Round to be crowned with the laurels of victory!

—description from the publisher
families: Misc: Watch It Played How To Videos

ai.summary: Khôra is a dice-driven engine-builder where you pick 2 of 7 actions each round and must adapt your plan to the die roll you get, climbing tracks that snowball into stronger resources, cards, and points. It plays fast for its depth, with tight turns and a real puzzle in reconciling your strategy with variable dice.
praised: Clever, tense action-selection puzzle balancing planned strategy against dice randomness
Multiple viable paths to victory (economy, military, culture, politics)
Fast turns and low downtime despite meaningful depth
Good component quality and iconography once learned
Strong replayability from varied strategies and achievement goals
criticised: Steep learning curve and dense rulebook/iconography for a first play
Dice manipulation mitigates but doesn't eliminate swingy bad rolls
Low direct player interaction can make it feel solitaire-ish
Some symbol/track overload makes teaching it to new players hard
End-of-game scoring can feel a bit fiddly to tally

interaction.kind: mostly parallel engine-building with light racing for shared resources/track positions

scoring.why: Points accumulate from multiple tracks, achievements, and end-game bonuses tied to how far you advanced across economy, culture, and military development

name: The King Is Dead: Second Edition
description:
The King is dead. The kingdom is divided. Three factions — the Scottish, the Welsh, and the English — vie for control and, across the sea, foreign invaders prepare to take advantage of the chaos. Players must marshal their limited resources to influence this power struggle, while ensuring that the faction that rises to dominate the realm favors them above all other claimants to the throne.

The King is Dead: Second Edition refreshes the accessible yet strikingly deep game with updated graphic design, gorgeous new artwork, and a brand-new asymmetric game mode for advanced play.
families: Misc: Watch It Played How To Videos

ai.summary: A tight two-to-four-player area-majority game where players secretly place influence cubes to sway which of three factions (or all four with foreign invaders) will control regions, then race to remember what everyone actually committed since much of it is played face-down. It plays fast and mean, with a distinctive memory element that rewards tracking opponents' hidden bids as much as spatial strategy.
praised: Clever memory mechanic where you must recall face-down/hidden commitments rather than rely on open information
Tight, fast playtime (30-45 min) with high replayability from variable setup
Elegant, minimalist design that hides real depth
Strong player interaction and tension despite the small footprint
Second edition's improved components, art, and the new asymmetric advanced mode
criticised: Memory requirement can frustrate players who dislike memory-based mechanics or feel it punishes forgetfulness over strategy
Rules and interactions (especially multi-faction/backstab dynamics) take a play or two to click
Can feel swingy or kingmaker-ish in some player counts, especially with only 2-3 factions in play
Relatively abstract/dry theme layered thinly onto the mechanics

interaction.kind: blocking, hidden bidding, and area-majority maneuvering with a memory-tracking element

scoring.why: The winner is determined by which faction ends up dominant and whether that outcome favors your secretly held allegiances, not by accumulating points from multiple sources

ai._name: The King Is Dead: Second Edition

name: King of Tokyo
description:
In King of Tokyo, you play mutant monsters, gigantic robots, and strange aliens—all of whom are destroying Tokyo and whacking each other in order to become the one and only King of Tokyo.

At the start of each turn, you roll six dice, which show the following six symbols: 1, 2, or 3 Victory Points, Energy, Heal, and Attack. Over three successive throws, choose whether to keep or discard each die in order to win victory points, gain energy, restore health, or attack other players into understanding that Tokyo is YOUR territory.

The fiercest player will occupy Tokyo, and earn extra victory points, but that player can't heal and must face all the other monsters alone!

Top this off with special cards purchased with energy that have a permanent or temporary effect, such as the growing of a second head which grants you an additional die, body armor, nova death ray, and more.... and it's one of the most explosive games of the year!

In order to win the game, one must either destroy Tokyo by accumulating 20 victory points, or be the only surviving monster once the fighting has ended.

First Game in the King of Tokyo series
families: Misc: Dice Tower Hall of Fame

ai.summary: A fast, loud dice-chucker where you push your luck rolling and re-rolling for points, energy, and attacks while whoever occupies Tokyo racks up bonus points but can't heal. Games are short, swingy, and driven by table talk and gang-up dynamics rather than deep strategy.
praised: Fast, easy to teach, great gateway/family game
Fun push-your-luck dice mechanic
Thematic monster/kaiju presentation and components
Card market adds variety and replayability
Plays well with kids and non-gamers
criticised: High luck/randomness can undercut player agency
Player elimination can leave people sitting out
Ganging up on the Tokyo occupant can feel mean or kingmaker-y
Shallow long-term strategy once the novelty wears off

interaction.kind: open conflict via dice attacks and take-that ganging up on whoever is in Tokyo

scoring.why: The winner is decided by racing to 20 victory points (mostly from dice and Tokyo occupancy) or by being the last monster standing after eliminating everyone else.

name: Kingdomino
description:
Kingdomino is a tile-laying game in which players take the role of monarchs expanding their kingdoms by claiming and arranging lands. Over the course of the game, players build a compact kingdom from forests, lakes, wheat fields, grasslands, swamps, and mines, carefully connecting matching terrain types while planning for valuable crown symbols that increase the prestige of their territories.

Each round, players place the domino they selected on the previous turn, following placement rules that require at least one matching terrain connection (or connection to the starting castle tile). After placing a domino, they choose a new one from the available row for a future turn. The order in which dominoes are chosen also determines the turn order for the next round, creating a balance between claiming the most desirable tiles and securing an earlier turn.

At the end of the game, players score each connected territory by multiplying its number of squares by the number of crowns within that territory. Territories without crowns score no points. The player with the highest total score wins, with ties broken first by the size of the largest territory, then by the total number of crowns.

—description from the publisher
families: Misc: Watch It Played How To Videos
Versions & Editions: Bigger Versions of Regular-Size Games

ai.summary: Kingdomino plays fast and light: each turn you draft a domino and place it to grow a compact 5x5 kingdom, weighing terrain matches against crown-heavy tiles. It's a satisfying little optimization puzzle that resolves in well under half an hour, with almost no downtime.
praised: Extremely easy to teach and fast to play
Elegant turn-order-as-drafting-priority mechanism
Satisfying spatial puzzle for its weight
Great gateway/family game and works well with kids
High production value components (chunky wooden tiles in the deluxe edition)
criticised: Very light strategic depth, can feel too simple for gamers
Luck of the draw/tile order can swing outcomes
Limited long-term replayability for experienced gamers
Interaction is indirect and can feel solitaire-ish at low player counts

interaction.kind: indirect drafting/denial via turn order and tile choice

ai.win_criteria: Most points, one or two sources

scoring.why: the winner is decided almost entirely by maximizing (territory size x crowns) across connected same-terrain regions

name: Kraftwagen: Age of Engineering
description:
Despite the fact that the North American automobile industry developed later than in Europe, the innovations in the mass production of vehicles and the immense internal market made the American automobile industry the largest and most powerful in the world.

In Kraftwagen: Age of Engineering, you will push the development of new engines and bodies with which to launch the best possible range of vehicles on the market, and you will have the opportunity to demonstrate the power of your engines in the first Grand Prix that were held in American territory.

Kraftwagen: Age of Engineering reimplements the original design by Matthias Cramer with improvements and simplifications that lessen the luck factor.

Let the roar of the engines resound, let the design of the new models attract buyers from all corners of the world, and get the prestige necessary to become the most famous car builder.

—description from the publisher

ai.summary: Players use a rondel to select actions each turn, researching and combining engines and bodies to build a competitive lineup of cars, then cash in on sales and race prestige. It's a tight, plan-ahead economic game where the rondel forces you to sequence actions efficiently rather than freely picking whatever you want.
praised: Clever, tense rondel action-selection mechanism
Satisfying engine/body combination puzzle for building cars
This edition trims luck and streamlines the fiddly original
Good component quality and thematic car-building feel
criticised: Rondel can feel restrictive or fiddly to learn at first
Racing element is a smaller, sometimes underwhelming part of the game
Can run long and a bit dry/mechanical for a car-racing theme
Niche reimplementation with less table presence than flashier economic games

interaction.kind: indirect competition over shared rondel spaces and market/race positions

scoring.why: Points come mainly from selling well-designed cars and race results, with prestige/money conversions layered on top

name: Kutná Hora: The City of Silver
description:
Join other ambitious guild leaders in mining and developing the famous City of Silver during its period of rapid economic growth and expansion in the 14th century — from the first discovery of silver near the Cistercian monastery to the construction of Kutná Hora, which quickly became one of the most important cities in central Europe.

Kutná Hora: The City of Silver is a historical city-building Eurogame for 2-4 players that features a real-life supply and demand experience in which every action you take has an impact on the game's dynamic economic systems.

In each round, players take turns selecting actions from a hand of double-sided cards to engage strategic plans like mining, purchasing plots of land on which to build, gaining permits, raising buildings for their affiliated guilds, gaining profit from their production, and of course working towards the construction of Saint Barbara's Cathedral.

The asymmetrical nature of each player's available guilds makes for highly interactive rounds in which each decision impacts the economy and other players in interesting ways as they expand their mines and build infrastructure across a shared board.

Mine ore and smelt it into a fortune of silver for expanding this beautiful historic city, but take care to balance your personal goal advancement with the need to further the city's growth. Everything is connected, and sometimes the path to personal victory relies on the prosperity of the many.

—description from publisher

ai.summary: A dense, systems-heavy Euro where you queue actions via double-sided cards and watch nearly every move ripple through a shared supply-and-demand market for resources like ore, stone, and permits. Turns are quick individually, but the payoff comes from reading the whole board's economy and timing your mining, building, and cathedral contributions before rivals shift prices against you.
praised: The dynamic market/pricing system feels genuinely reactive and clever rather than bolted-on
Strong sense of economic interdependence — other players' actions visibly affect your options
Asymmetric guild powers give replayability and distinct strategies
Satisfying long-term puzzle of sequencing actions on the card queue
criticised: Steep rules overhead and a fiddly first few plays before the systems click
Iconography and card-queue mechanism can feel unintuitive early on
Can run long, especially at 4 players, with some downtime between turns
Production/component quality and rulebook clarity drew some complaints at launch

name: Lost Cities
description:
Lost Cities is a card game in the Kosmos two-player series. The game originally consisted of a single deck of cards of rank 2–10 in five different colors with three special "handshakes" ("HS" in scoring examples below) in each suit, but as of 2018 the game now includes six colored suits, with the sixth color being optional for gameplay. A game board is included to organize discarded cards and help players organize their card collections.

The object of the game is to gain points by mounting profitable archaeological expeditions to the different sites represented by the colored suits of cards. On a player's turn, they must first play one card, either to an expedition or by discarding it to the color-appropriate discard pile, then draw one card, either from the deck or from the top of a discard pile. Cards played to expeditions must be in ascending order, but they need not be consecutive. Handshakes are considered lower than a 2 and represent investments in an expedition. Thus, if you play a red 4, you may play any other red card higher than a 4 on a future turn but may no longer play a handshake, the 2, or the 3.

The game continues in this fashion with players alternating turns until the final card is taken from the deck. The rest of the cards in hand are then discarded and players score their expeditions. Each expedition that has at least one card played into it must be scored. Cards played into an expedition are worth their rank in points, and handshakes count as a multiplier against your final total; one handshake doubles an expedition's value, while two handshakes triples that value and three handshakes quadruple it. Expeditions start at a value of -20, so you must play at least 20 points of cards into an expedition in order to make a profit. If you are left with a negative value and have a handshake, the multiplier still applies. A 20-point bonus is awarded to every expedition with at least eight cards played into it. A complete game of Lost Cities lasts three matches, with scores for each match being added together.

Scoring example 1: An expedition has a 2,3,7,8,10 for a total of 30. This expedition is worth 10 total points: 30 plus the initial -20.

Scoring example 2: An expedition has 2 HS, and 4,5,6,7,8,10 for a total of 40. This expedition is worth 80 total points: 40 points for cards, plus the initial -20, ×3 for the two multipliers, plus the 20-pt bonus for playing 8+ cards.

Scoring example 3: An expedition has 1 HS, and 4,6,7 for a total of 17. This expedition is worth -6 total points: 17 plus the initial -20, ×2 for the multiplier.

name: Mandala
description:
The Mandala: the symbol of an ancient and sacred ritual. Colored sand is laid to create a symbolic map of the world before the pattern is ceremonially destroyed and the sand cast into the river.

In the two-player game Mandala, you are trying to score more than your opponent by collecting valuable cards — but you won't know which cards are valuable until well into the game! Over the course of the game, players play their colored cards into the two mandalas, building the central shared mountains and laying cards into their own fields. As soon as a mandala has all six colors, the players take turns choosing the colors in the mountain and adding those cards to their "river" and "cup". At the end of the game, the cards in your cup are worth points based on the position of their colors in that player's river. The player whose cup is worth more points wins.

The linen playmat shows two circular mandalas, with each being divided by a horizontal space (the mountain) to create one "field" for each player. The playmat has seven spaces in front of each player to hold their river of single face-up cards and their cup: the stack of face-down cards which they score at the end of the game.

To begin, each player receives a hand of six cards. Each player receives two random cards face down in their cup, then two random cards are dealt face up into the central mountain strip of each mandala.

On your turn, you may play either a single card into one of the mountains, or one or more matching cards into one of your fields. All cards played into a mandala must follow the "Rule of Color": Once a color has been played into one of the three areas of a mandala, then later cards of the same color can be played only into that same area. Thus, once your opponent has played red cards into their field, then you can't play red cards in your field, and neither you nor your opponent can play red cards into the central mountain. If you played a card into a mountain, draw three new cards from the deck at the end of your turn; if you played cards into one of your fields, do not draw new cards.

A mandala is completed once it contains all six colors of cards. When this happens, the players "destroy" the mandala, taking turns to choose a color present in the mountain and claim all cards of that color. Whoever played more cards in their field chooses first; if tied, the player who did not complete the mandala chooses first. The first time you claim cards of a specific color, lay one of these cards in the lowest-valued empty space in your river, then place the rest into your cup. The spaces in your river are valued 1-6 in order, so cards of the first color you claim will be worth 1 point each, cards of the second color you claim are worth 2 points each, and so on.

Once a mandala has been destroyed and all the colors in the mountain claimed, cards played in the fields are discarded, two new cards are dealt face up into the mountain, and the game continues.

The end of the game is triggered either when the deck is exhausted or when one player adds a sixth color to their river. Both players then tally the value of all the cards in their cup, based on the position of the colors in their river, and whoever has the higher score wins!

Contents:

     1 linen playmat
     108 mandala cards (18 in each of 6 colours)
     2 reference cards
